gd.enable_tbl_preview(n_head=8, n_tail=3)

Many practical problems turn into a question about choosing nodes or edges under a rule. Exams
that share a student can't be held at the same time. Each worker takes one task. Every link of a
network must be watched by a monitor at one of its ends. These are the classic problems of
*coloring*, *matching*, and *covering*, and this page shows how to state them as graphs and solve
them with EdgeCase.

Several of these problems are NP-hard: no known method solves them exactly and quickly on large
graphs. For those, EdgeCase provides fast heuristics, some with guaranteed bounds, and this page
shows how to judge the quality of an answer. Every kind of solution also has a checker, such as
`is_valid_coloring()` or `is_vertex_cover()`, which tests an answer from any source. The last
section covers structural tests (bipartite, planar, chordal) that tell when a hard problem becomes
easy.

## Coloring

### Scheduling with colors

A *coloring* gives each node a color so that no two linked nodes share one. If the nodes are exams
and the edges join exams that some student must take both of, then each color is a time slot in
which the exams can run together without a clash. The fewest colors that work, the *chromatic
number*, is the shortest possible exam timetable.

The conflict graph is built from the enrollments, with an edge for each pair of courses that a
student takes together. `simplify()` then merges the edges that several students produce:

```{python}
import edgecase as ec
import polars as pl
from itertools import combinations

enrollments = {
    "Avery": ["Algebra", "Biology", "Chemistry"],
    "Blake": ["Algebra", "Drama"],
    "Casey": ["Biology", "Economics", "French"],
    "Devon": ["Chemistry", "French"],
    "Emery": ["Drama", "Geography", "History"],
    "Finley": ["Economics", "History"],
    "Harper": ["Algebra", "French", "Geography"],
    "Jordan": ["Biology", "History"],
}

conflicts = ec.Graph()
for courses in enrollments.values():
    conflicts.add_edges(list(combinations(courses, 2)), auto_create_nodes=True)
conflicts.simplify()
conflicts.count_nodes(), conflicts.count_edges()
```

Eight courses have 16 conflicting pairs.
[`greedy_color()`](../reference/Graph.greedy_color.qmd) colors the nodes and returns a dictionary
from node ID to color, numbered from 0. Grouping the courses by color gives the timetable:

```{python}
slots = conflicts.greedy_color()

timetable = {}
for node, slot in sorted(slots.items(), key=lambda item: item[1]):
    timetable.setdefault(slot, []).append(conflicts.get_label_from_id(node))
timetable
```

Four slots are enough. Storing the colors as a node attribute and plotting by it shows that no
edge joins two nodes of the same color:

```{python}
conflicts.set_node_attrs("slot", slots)
conflicts.plot(color_by="slot", label_by="label", seed=2, width=500, height=400)
```

[`is_valid_coloring()`](../reference/Graph.is_valid_coloring.qmd) checks the rule for any coloring,
such as one edited by hand to suit a constraint the graph doesn't capture.

### How good is a coloring?

The greedy algorithm visits the nodes one at a time and gives each the smallest color that none of
its neighbors has. The result is always valid, but it may use more colors than necessary, so its
count is an *upper bound* on the chromatic number.
[`chromatic_number_upper_bound()`](../reference/Graph.chromatic_number_upper_bound.qmd) returns the
number of colors in a coloring.

A *lower bound* comes from cliques. The members of a clique are all linked to each other, so each
needs its own color, and the chromatic number is at least the size of the largest clique. When the
two bounds meet, the coloring is optimal:

```{python}
(
    conflicts.chromatic_number_upper_bound(slots),
    conflicts.clique_number(),
    [conflicts.get_label_from_id(node) for node in conflicts.maximum_clique()],
)
```

Algebra, Biology, Chemistry, and French conflict pairwise, since every pair of them shares a
student, so no timetable can have fewer than four slots, and the greedy one is optimal.

The clique bound is not always tight. The *Mycielski graphs* have no triangles at all, so their
largest clique has only two nodes, yet they need ever more colors. The fourth of them, the
Grötzsch graph, needs four:

```{python}
grotzsch = ec.Graph().add_mycielski_graph(n=4)
grotzsch.clique_number(), grotzsch.chromatic_number_upper_bound()
```

When the bounds differ, the true chromatic number lies between them, and finding it exactly is
NP-hard. Without a coloring argument, `chromatic_number_upper_bound()` colors the graph itself with
the default greedy strategy.

### Coloring strategies

The order in which the greedy algorithm visits the nodes decides how many colors it uses, and
`strategy=` chooses the order. The default, `"largest_first"`, colors high-degree nodes first,
since they are the hardest to fit in later. `"dsatur"` picks, at each step, the node whose
neighbors already use the most distinct colors, and usually does best. On a random graph of 200
nodes:

```{python}
random_graph = ec.Graph().add_gnp_graph(n=200, p=0.1, seed=2)
strategies = ["largest_first", "smallest_last", "dsatur", "independent_set", "random"]
{
    strategy: random_graph.chromatic_number_upper_bound(
        random_graph.greedy_color(strategy=strategy, seed=1)
    )
    for strategy in strategies
}
```

DSATUR and the independent-set strategy, which builds one color class at a time, use eight colors,
while a random order needs eleven. With `interchange=True`, the greedy algorithm tries to avoid
opening a new color by swapping two existing colors along a chain of nodes, which often closes much
of the gap:

```{python}
random_graph.chromatic_number_upper_bound(random_graph.greedy_color(interchange=True))
```

Since the strategies are fast, the practical approach on a hard instance is to try several and
keep the coloring with the fewest colors.

### Coloring intervals

Some graphs are easy to color exactly. In an *interval graph*, each node is a span of time, and
two nodes are linked when their spans overlap. A day of meetings is one: each color is a meeting
room, and the chromatic number is the number of rooms the day needs.
[`add_interval_graph()`](../reference/Graph.add_interval_graph.qmd) builds the graph from the
intervals, which are closed, so two meetings that merely touch (one ending at 11:00 and the next
starting at 11:00) count as overlapping:

```{python}
meetings = {
    "Standup": (9.0, 9.25),
    "Design review": (9.5, 11.0),
    "Hiring panel": (10.0, 12.0),
    "Budget": (10.5, 11.5),
    "Planning": (11.75, 13.0),
    "Lunch talk": (12.25, 13.25),
    "One-on-one": (13.5, 14.5),
    "Retro": (14.0, 15.0),
}
day = ec.Graph().add_interval_graph(list(meetings.values()))
day.relabel_nodes(dict(enumerate(meetings, start=1)))

rooms = {}
for node, room in sorted(day.greedy_color(strategy="dsatur").items(), key=lambda item: item[1]):
    rooms.setdefault(room, []).append(day.get_label_from_id(node))
rooms, day.clique_number()
```

Three rooms are enough, and three are needed, since the design review, the hiring panel, and the
budget meeting are all in progress between 10:30 and 11:00. For interval graphs the two bounds
always meet: the chromatic number equals the size of the largest clique, which is the greatest
number of intervals that overlap at any moment. This makes interval graphs an example of the
*perfect* graphs described [below](#graph-classes).

### Edge coloring

An *edge coloring* colors the edges instead, so that the edges at each node all differ. Each color
is then a set of edges with no node in common, which can all happen at once. In a round-robin
tournament, the teams are nodes, the games are edges, and each color is a round in which every team
plays at most once. [`edge_coloring()`](../reference/Graph.edge_coloring.qmd) maps each edge ID to
a color:

```{python}
teams = ["Ajax", "Benfica", "Celtic", "Dynamo", "Everton"]
league = ec.Graph().add_nodes(teams).add_edges(list(combinations(teams, 2)))

label = league.get_label_from_id
games = {edge: (label(home), label(away)) for edge, home, away in league.get_edges_as_tuples()}

schedule = {}
for edge, matchday in sorted(league.edge_coloring().items(), key=lambda item: item[1]):
    schedule.setdefault(matchday, []).append(games[edge])
schedule
```

The ten games fit into five rounds of two games, and in each round the fifth team rests. A node
with `d` edges needs `d` colors around it, so at least as many colors as the highest degree are
needed. The method always uses at most one more than that; with five teams of degree four, five
rounds is the best possible, since an odd number of teams can't all play in the same round.
[`is_valid_edge_coloring()`](../reference/Graph.is_valid_edge_coloring.qmd) checks an edge
coloring.

## Matching

### Pairs of nodes

A *matching* is a set of edges with no node in common, so that each node is paired with at most one
partner. Pairing students for a project, donors with recipients, or players into doubles teams are
all matching problems, where the edges say which pairs are possible. A *maximal* matching can't be
extended by another edge, while a *maximum* matching has the most edges of any matching. The two
differ, as the karate club shows:

```{python}
karate = ec.karate_club()
best = karate.maximum_weight_matching()
quick = karate.maximal_matching()
len(best), len(quick), karate.is_perfect_matching(best)
```

[`maximal_matching()`](../reference/Graph.maximal_matching.qmd) takes edges greedily and stops at 11
pairs of friends, but [`maximum_weight_matching()`](../reference/Graph.maximum_weight_matching.qmd)
finds 13. That still leaves 8 of the 34 members without a partner, so the club has no *perfect*
matching, one that pairs everyone. Half of the members have three friends or fewer, and most of
those friendships lead to the same few central members, such as the instructor, the administrator,
and member `"32"`. Each of them can be in only one pair, so many of their friends are left out.

On a weighted graph, `maximum_weight_matching()` maximizes the total weight of the pairs. In the
*Les Misérables* network, the weight of an edge is the number of chapters in which two characters
appear together, so the matching pairs characters by the strength of their ties:

```{python}
miserables = ec.les_miserables()
pairs = miserables.maximum_weight_matching()

label = miserables.get_label_from_id
(
    miserables.get_edge_df()
    .filter(pl.col("id").is_in(pairs))
    .sort("weight", descending=True)
    .select(
        pl.col("source").map_elements(label, return_dtype=pl.String),
        pl.col("target").map_elements(label, return_dtype=pl.String),
        "weight",
    )
)
```

The strongest pairs are Marius and Cosette, Javert and Valjean, and the Thénardiers. Valjean's
strongest tie is with Cosette, but she is better paired with Marius, and the matching gives Valjean
to Javert instead: it maximizes the total, not each pair. By default the matching ignores the
number of pairs. With `maxcardinality=True`, it first pairs as many nodes as possible and only then
maximizes the weight:

```{python}
def total_weight(graph, edges):
    return graph.get_edge_df().filter(pl.col("id").is_in(edges))["weight"].sum()


widest = miserables.maximum_weight_matching(maxcardinality=True)
len(pairs), total_weight(miserables, pairs), len(widest), total_weight(miserables, widest)
```

Pairing six more characters costs a third of the total weight, since many of the remaining
characters have only weak ties to anyone still free.
[`minimum_weight_matching()`](../reference/Graph.minimum_weight_matching.qmd) is the opposite
problem, the cheapest of the matchings with the most pairs, for weights that are costs.
`method="greedy"` gives a faster approximate matching for very large graphs.

### Assignment

In a *bipartite* graph, the nodes fall into two groups and every edge joins the two, as with
workers and tasks. Finding the cheapest way to give each task its own worker is the *assignment
problem*, and [`bipartite_minimum_weight_full_matching()`](../reference/Graph.bipartite_minimum_weight_full_matching.qmd)
solves it. The edges are the pairings that are allowed, weighted by their cost, here the hours that
each translator needs for each part of a project:

```{python}
hours = [
    ("Ana", "Translation", 9),
    ("Ana", "Editing", 4),
    ("Ana", "Layout", 6),
    ("Ben", "Translation", 5),
    ("Ben", "Editing", 7),
    ("Ben", "Layout", 8),
    ("Cleo", "Translation", 7),
    ("Cleo", "Editing", 3),
    ("Cleo", "Layout", 5),
    ("Dev", "Editing", 6),
    ("Dev", "Layout", 2),
]
project = ec.Graph(weighted=True).add_edges(hours, auto_create_nodes=True)
assigned = project.bipartite_minimum_weight_full_matching()

label = project.get_label_from_id
[
    (label(source), label(target))
    for edge, source, target in project.get_edges_as_tuples()
    if edge in assigned
], total_weight(project, assigned)
```

The work takes 10 hours with Ben translating, Cleo editing, and Dev on layout. Every node on the
smaller side, here the three tasks, gets a partner, so Ana is left without a task. The graph must be
created with `weighted=True`, otherwise every pairing would count as equally costly (see
[The graph model](03-graph-model.qmd)). To maximize a total score instead of minimizing a cost,
negate the weights.

### Why a matching can't be larger

Without weights, [`bipartite_maximum_matching()`](../reference/Graph.bipartite_maximum_matching.qmd)
finds the most pairs with the fast Hopcroft-Karp algorithm. Suppose five students list the
projects they would accept:

```{python}
choices = {
    "Ana": ["Robotics", "Vision"],
    "Ben": ["Robotics", "Vision"],
    "Cleo": ["Robotics", "Vision"],
    "Dev": ["Vision", "Compilers", "Databases"],
    "Eli": ["Compilers"],
}
projects = ec.Graph().add_edges(
    [(student, choice) for student, options in choices.items() for choice in options],
    auto_create_nodes=True,
)
students = list(choices)

label = projects.get_label_from_id
placed = projects.bipartite_maximum_matching(top_nodes=students)
cover = projects.bipartite_vertex_cover(top_nodes=students)
len(placed), [label(node) for node in cover]
```

At most four students can be placed. The reason is in the *vertex cover*, a set of nodes that
touches every edge, returned by
[`bipartite_vertex_cover()`](../reference/Graph.bipartite_vertex_cover.qmd). Every acceptable
pairing involves Robotics, Vision, Dev, or Eli, and each of these four can be in only one pair, so
no matching can have more than four pairs. By König's theorem, in a bipartite graph the largest
matching and the smallest vertex cover always have the same size, so the cover is a certificate
that the matching can't be improved. Here it points at the bottleneck: Ana, Ben, and Cleo compete
for two projects. `top_nodes=` names one side of the graph; without it, the sides are found
automatically.

## Covers, independent sets, and dominating sets

A small family of problems asks for a set of nodes that relates to the rest of the graph in a
particular way:

| Problem | The chosen nodes must | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Vertex cover | touch every edge | monitors that watch every link |
| Independent set | include no two linked nodes | a committee with no conflicts of interest |
| Dominating set | be linked to every node not chosen | facilities within reach of every town |

All three are NP-hard in general. EdgeCase provides fast heuristics, and checkers that test any
candidate set.

### Vertex covers and independent sets

[`minimum_weighted_vertex_cover()`](../reference/Graph.minimum_weighted_vertex_cover.qmd) finds a
vertex cover that is guaranteed to be at most twice the size of the smallest. With
`node_weight_attr=`, it minimizes the total of a node attribute, such as the cost of installing a
monitor at each node, instead of the number of nodes. An *independent set* is the opposite: a set of
nodes with no edges among them.
[`maximum_independent_set()`](../reference/Graph.maximum_independent_set.qmd) finds a large one by
taking low-degree nodes first:

```{python}
cover = karate.minimum_weighted_vertex_cover()
independent = karate.maximum_independent_set()
len(cover), karate.is_vertex_cover(cover), len(independent), karate.is_independent_set(independent)
```

The two problems are two views of one. If a set of nodes is independent, every edge has at least
one end outside it, so the nodes outside it form a vertex cover. The 20 independent members
therefore give a cover of 14, better than the 17 found directly:

```{python}
others = [node for node in range(1, 35) if node not in independent]
len(others), karate.is_vertex_cover(others)
```

Comparing heuristics in this way, and checking the result with
[`is_vertex_cover()`](../reference/Graph.is_vertex_cover.qmd) or
[`is_independent_set()`](../reference/Graph.is_independent_set.qmd), is good practice whenever an
exact answer is out of reach. On a bipartite graph, `bipartite_vertex_cover()` finds the exact
minimum, as in the previous section.

A *maximal* independent set can't be extended, but may be much smaller than the largest.
[`maximal_independent_set()`](../reference/Graph.maximal_independent_set.qmd) builds one in a
random order, and
[`find_maximal_independent_sets()`](../reference/Graph.find_maximal_independent_sets.qmd) builds
several, which shows how much they vary:

```{python}
[len(group) for group in karate.find_maximal_independent_sets(count=10, seed=1)]
```

The ten sets range from 15 to 20 members. Random restarts like these are a simple way to search for
a larger set.

[`minimum_edge_cover()`](../reference/Graph.minimum_edge_cover.qmd) is the edge version of a cover:
the fewest edges that touch every node. It is exact, and it is closely tied to matching: the karate
club's 13 pairs cover 26 members with 13 edges, and each of the other 8 members needs one more edge,
for 21 in all:

```{python}
len(karate.minimum_edge_cover())
```

### Dominating sets

A *dominating set* is a set of nodes such that every other node is linked to at least one of them,
like a set of stations within one step of every town, or a few members who can pass a message
directly to everyone else in the club.
[`minimum_weighted_dominating_set()`](../reference/Graph.minimum_weighted_dominating_set.qmd) looks
for a small one, preferring nodes that cover many others, while the simpler
[`dominating_set()`](../reference/Graph.dominating_set.qmd) sweeps the nodes in ID order:

```{python}
hubs = karate.minimum_weighted_dominating_set()
len(karate.dominating_set()), [karate.get_label_from_id(node) for node in hubs]
```

The sweep needs 13 members, but four are enough: the instructor (`"0"`), the administrator
(`"33"`), and members `"5"` and `"24"`, who reach the members that neither leader knows.
[`is_dominating_set()`](../reference/Graph.is_dominating_set.qmd) confirms the result, and the plot
shows that every other member is next to one of the four:

```{python}
karate.set_node_attrs("dominating", {node: node in hubs for node in range(1, 35)})
karate.plot(color_by="dominating", label_by="label", seed=1)
```

With `node_weight_attr=`, the method minimizes a total cost instead, for example when some sites are
more expensive to build on than others.

## Maximum cut

The *maximum cut* splits the nodes into two sides so that as many edges as possible cross between
them. It models dividing people into two teams so that rivals end up on opposite sides, or
assigning the parts of a circuit to two layers so that as few wires as possible stay within one.
It is the opposite of community detection, which looks for groups with few edges between them.
[`maximum_cut()`](../reference/Graph.maximum_cut.qmd) returns the number of crossing edges (or their
total weight) and the two sides:

```{python}
cut_size, (side_a, side_b) = karate.maximum_cut(seed=1)

faction_1 = set(karate.get_node_df().filter(pl.col("faction") == 1)["id"].to_list())
across_factions = sum(
    (source in faction_1) != (target in faction_1)
    for _, source, target in karate.get_edges_as_tuples()
)
cut_size, len(side_a), len(side_b), across_factions
```

The cut found by the method has 61 of the club's 78 friendships crossing between a side of 9
members and a side of 25. The split into the two factions, by contrast, has only 10 friendships
across it, which is why it is a good community structure and a poor cut. Max-cut is NP-hard, and
the default method, a local search that moves one node at a time while that improves the cut, is
guaranteed to cut at least half of the edges. `method="randomized"` assigns the sides at random,
and is mainly useful as a baseline.

## Graph classes

Some kinds of graphs make hard problems easy, so it pays to know whether a graph belongs to one.
EdgeCase has tests for the most useful classes.

### Bipartite graphs

A graph is *bipartite* when its nodes can be split into two sides with every edge between them,
which is the same as being colorable with two colors, or having no cycle of odd length.
[`is_bipartite()`](../reference/Graph.is_bipartite.qmd) tests this, and
[`bipartite_sets()`](../reference/Graph.bipartite_sets.qmd) returns the two sides:

```{python}
women_events = ec.davis_southern_women()
women, events = women_events.bipartite_sets()
women_events.is_bipartite(), len(women), len(events), karate.is_bipartite()
```

The Southern Women network splits into its 18 women and 14 events. The karate club is not
bipartite, since any triangle of friends is an odd cycle. The bipartite matching and cover methods
above require a bipartite graph, and [Transforming graphs](19-transforming.qmd#derived-graphs) shows
how to project one onto either side.

### Planar graphs

A graph is *planar* when it can be drawn on a page with no edges crossing, which matters for
circuit layout, for maps (where countries that share a border form a planar graph), and for the
many algorithms that are faster on planar inputs.
[`check_planarity()`](../reference/Graph.check_planarity.qmd) returns the answer together with the
evidence. For a planar graph, the evidence is an *embedding*: the neighbors of each node in
clockwise order around it. The cube is planar:

```{python}
cube = ec.Graph().add_hypercube_graph(3)
is_planar, embedding = cube.check_planarity()
is_planar, embedding[1], cube.planar_faces()
```

In the drawing described by the embedding, the edges divide the page into *faces*, and
[`planar_faces()`](../reference/Graph.planar_faces.qmd) lists the nodes around each. The cube has
six, its six sides, including the outer face that surrounds the drawing. Euler's formula ties the
counts together for any connected planar graph: nodes minus edges plus faces is 2, here
`8 - 12 + 6`.

For a graph that is not planar, `counterexample=True` returns the evidence of that: a *Kuratowski
subgraph*, a copy of one of the two smallest non-planar graphs (five nodes all linked, or three
nodes each linked to three others) with some edges possibly divided into paths:

```{python}
petersen = ec.Graph().add_named_graph("petersen")
is_planar, witness = petersen.check_planarity(counterexample=True)
is_planar, witness.count_nodes(), witness.count_edges(), witness.get_node_df()["degree"].to_list()
```

The Petersen graph is not planar. The witness has six nodes of degree three, which are the two
groups of three in the second pattern, and three nodes of degree two that lie on the subdivided
edges. Finding the witness reruns the test once for each edge, so it is slower than the plain
check; [`is_planar()`](../reference/Graph.is_planar.qmd) gives only the answer.
[`layout_planar()`](../reference/Graph.layout_planar.qmd) computes positions with no crossings
for a planar graph (see [Layouts](23-layouts.qmd)).

### Chordal graphs and treewidth

A graph is *chordal* when every cycle of four or more nodes has a *chord*, an edge between two of
its nodes that aren't next to each other on the cycle. Interval graphs, such as the meetings above,
are chordal, as are trees. Chordal graphs have few maximal cliques, at most one per node, and
[`chordal_graph_cliques()`](../reference/Graph.chordal_graph_cliques.qmd) lists them in linear
time:

```{python}
day.is_chordal(), [[day.get_label_from_id(node) for node in clique] for clique in day.chordal_graph_cliques()]
```

Each clique of the meeting graph is a set of meetings in progress at the same moment.

Most graphs are not chordal, but every graph can be made chordal by adding edges, and how few
are needed measures how far the graph is from being a tree. That measure is the *treewidth*. A tree
has treewidth 1, a cycle 2, and a complete graph of `n` nodes `n - 1`. Many NP-hard problems,
including coloring, independent sets, and inference in probabilistic models, can be solved
quickly on graphs of small treewidth, by dynamic programming over a *tree decomposition*: a tree
whose nodes are overlapping groups of the original nodes, called *bags*.
[`tree_decomposition()`](../reference/Graph.tree_decomposition.qmd) builds one with a heuristic and
returns its width, the size of its largest bag minus one, which is an upper bound on the treewidth:

```{python}
width, decomposition = karate.tree_decomposition()
width, decomposition.count_nodes(), decomposition.get_node_df()["label"].head(3).to_list()
```

The karate club has a decomposition of width 5, made of 29 bags, each labelled with its members.
The width stays small even on much larger sparse networks. The US power grid has 4,941 nodes but a
decomposition of width at most 19:

```{python}
ec.power_grid().tree_decomposition()[0]
```

`heuristic="min_degree"` uses a different elimination rule that is sometimes better.
[`complete_to_chordal_graph()`](../reference/Graph.complete_to_chordal_graph.qmd) adds a minimal set
of edges that makes a graph chordal, and
[`chordal_graph_treewidth()`](../reference/Graph.chordal_graph_treewidth.qmd) gives the exact
treewidth of a chordal graph. The junction trees used for exact inference in Bayesian networks are
tree decompositions of the moral graph (see [Directed acyclic graphs](17-dags.qmd)).

### Perfect graphs and cographs

A graph is *perfect* when, in it and in every induced subgraph, the chromatic number equals the size
of the largest clique, so the clique bound from the start of this page is always exact. Bipartite
graphs, interval graphs, and chordal graphs are all perfect, and on perfect graphs the coloring,
clique, and independent set problems can all be solved in polynomial time.
[`is_perfect_graph()`](../reference/Graph.is_perfect_graph.qmd) tests the property:

```{python}
day.is_perfect_graph(), cube.is_perfect_graph(), grotzsch.is_perfect_graph()
```

The meeting graph and the cube are perfect. The Grötzsch graph is not, since its chromatic number
of four is above its clique number of two.

*Cographs* are the graphs that can be built from single nodes by repeatedly taking disjoint unions
and complements, and equivalently those with no induced path on four nodes.
[`is_cograph()`](../reference/Graph.is_cograph.qmd) tests for them, and
[`modular_decomposition()`](../reference/Graph.modular_decomposition.qmd) returns the tree that
describes how any graph breaks down into *modules*, groups of nodes that all have the same
neighbors outside the group.

## Summary

| Problem | Methods | Exact? |
|---|---|---|
| Node coloring | `greedy_color()`, `chromatic_number_upper_bound()`, `is_valid_coloring()` | Heuristic; check against `clique_number()` |
| Edge coloring | `edge_coloring()`, `is_valid_edge_coloring()` | At most one color above the optimum |
| Matching | `maximum_weight_matching()`, `minimum_weight_matching()`, `maximal_matching()`, `is_matching()`, `is_perfect_matching()` | Exact (except `maximal_matching()` and `method="greedy"`) |
| Bipartite matching | `bipartite_maximum_matching()`, `bipartite_minimum_weight_full_matching()` | Exact |
| Vertex cover | `minimum_weighted_vertex_cover()`, `bipartite_vertex_cover()`, `is_vertex_cover()` | Within a factor of two; exact on bipartite graphs |
| Edge cover | `minimum_edge_cover()`, `is_edge_cover()` | Exact |
| Independent set | `maximum_independent_set()`, `maximal_independent_set()`, `find_maximal_independent_sets()`, `is_independent_set()` | Heuristic |
| Dominating set | `minimum_weighted_dominating_set()`, `dominating_set()`, `is_dominating_set()` | Heuristic |
| Maximum cut | `maximum_cut()` | Heuristic; at least half the edges |
| Graph classes | `is_bipartite()`, `check_planarity()`, `is_chordal()`, `is_perfect_graph()`, `is_cograph()` | Exact |
| Treewidth | `tree_decomposition()`, `chordal_graph_treewidth()` | Upper bound; exact on chordal graphs |

The problems of finding routes through every node or edge (the traveling salesman problem, Euler
tours, and Steiner trees) are covered in [Paths and distances](12-paths.qmd).
